report:
**Conclusion:** “No” is too definitive. Magnesium *may* reduce depressive symptoms, but the evidence is preliminary and not strong enough to regard it as an established depression treatment.

A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of seven randomized trials (eight effect estimates) found lower depression scores with magnesium than control (standardized mean difference −0.919; 95% CI −1.443 to −0.396). However, the authors note that trial findings had been inconsistent. The small number of studies, differences in participants, magnesium preparations/doses, and study designs mean the apparent average benefit is uncertain and may not apply broadly.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/

One often-cited 2017 randomized trial found improvement in adults with mild-to-moderate depression using magnesium chloride (248 mg elemental magnesium/day), but this was an open-label crossover study—not a blinded placebo-controlled trial—so expectation and reporting effects could account for some or all of the benefit.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28654669/

Major depression guidance such as NICE recommends evidence-based psychological treatments, antidepressants when appropriate, and other clinical interventions; magnesium is not a recommended standard treatment.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng222

Magnesium supplements are not risk-free: NIH notes diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal cramping at higher supplemental intakes, possible drug interactions, and greater toxicity risk with impaired kidney function.  
https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/

**Practical takeaway:** correcting a documented deficiency is sensible with a clinician’s advice, but magnesium should not replace assessment or established treatment for depression. Seek urgent help if depression includes suicidal thoughts or inability to stay safe.
